record.paper_title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era: A personal vision
record.context_brief: NLP and program-synthesis approaches to morphological AI
record.original_question: For morphological artificial intelligence based on a morphological language of operators and structuring elements, what coding is most appropriate for natural-language-processing techniques, should operators and structuring elements be represented as inflected forms or separate words, what decomposition granularity preserves semantic interpretability while remaining learnable, is there a large enough corpus of morphological programs to learn operator embeddings, how can programs be extracted and parsed from multiple repositories, how can syntactical transformations simplify and rewrite morphological programs, and how can combinatorial and deep-learning techniques be integrated to search large program spaces efficiently?

evidence.quote: What is the most appropiate coding of the morphological language to be use with NLP techniques? Is it efficient to use a word for the operator and a declination for the structuring element? Or to use different words for operator and structuring element? What is the optimal granularity on the decomposition of the operators to obtain a language with a high enough semantic interpretation and which can be still learnt? Do we have a large enough corpus of morphological programs available to learn the operator2vect embeddings? How to extract and parse morphological programs available in multiple repositories to train the algorithms? How can one introduce syntactical transformations to simplify and rewrite a morphological program? How to integrate combinatorial and deep learning techniques to explore large enough program spaces which can provide an efficient morphological AI?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider mathematical morphology, in which images are processed by operators built from a small set of primitive operations (e.g., erosion, dilation, opening, closing, geodesic reconstruction, hit-or-miss) combined with structuring elements (subsets of the underlying lattice that parameterize each operation). A "morphological program" is a finite composition (or more generally, a syntactic expression over a formal grammar) of such operators applied to structuring elements; the set of all such programs forms a formal language L whose tokens are operator symbols and structuring-element descriptors.

The goal is to develop a "morphological artificial intelligence" that learns and synthesizes morphological programs by combining natural-language-processing (NLP) techniques (token embeddings, sequence models) with combinatorial program-space search. Formalize and address the following questions:

1. Tokenization/coding: Define a coding scheme c : L → Σ* of morphological programs into a finite alphabet Σ that is best suited for NLP-style learning. In particular, decide whether structuring elements should be encoded as inflectional modifiers of operator tokens (a single token for "operator + structuring element" with morphological declensions) or as separate tokens (operator token and structuring-element token treated independently), and quantify the trade-off in expressivity vs. learnability.

2. Granularity: Determine the optimal decomposition granularity of compound operators into atomic sub-operators so that the resulting language has (a) high semantic interpretability (each token corresponds to a human-meaningful operation) and (b) is statistically learnable from finite data.

3. Corpus: Establish whether there exists a sufficiently large corpus C ⊂ L of morphological programs to train distributional embeddings (an "operator2vec" map φ : Σ → R^d) with provable approximation guarantees, and characterize the minimum corpus size as a function of vocabulary size and embedding dimension.

4. Extraction/parsing: Provide an algorithm for extracting and parsing morphological programs from heterogeneous source repositories into a normalized abstract syntax tree representation suitable for training.

5. Syntactic rewriting: Construct a confluent (or near-confluent) rewriting system R over L whose rewrite rules are semantics-preserving (i.e., for every program p, the rewritten program R(p) computes the same image transformation) and which simplifies programs in a useful normal form.

6. Hybrid search: Design an algorithm that integrates combinatorial program-space search (e.g., enumeration, SMT, genetic methods) with learned neural priors (sequence models trained on C using φ) to efficiently explore the program space and synthesize a morphological program matching a given input–output specification.

Provide constructions, theoretical guarantees, and/or impossibility results addressing each of the six points above.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as a research program/open direction concerning morphological AI based on a formal language of operators and structuring elements combined with NLP-style learning. No published work has been found that resolves the coding, granularity, corpus-existence, parsing, rewriting, and hybrid search questions in this framework; the topic remains an open research direction.

status_evidence.title: Some open questions on morphological operators and representations in the deep learning era
status_evidence.snippet: A personal vision listing open questions about morphological operators, including NLP-based morphological AI.
status_evidence.claim: The questions are stated as open research directions.
